speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have prepared answers to some of the questions which have been brought up during the session and upon which I expect hon. members would like to have information. With your permission, Mr. Chairman, I shall stay rather close to my notes in placing that information on Hansard.
Net income to farmers from the sale of farm products reached a peak of $2-2 billion in 1951. Estimates for the net income received in 1952 are placed at just under $2 billion. There is some indication that this present satisfactory position may be maintained. The cost of equipment and materials used in agricultural production reached a peak in 1952 and has declined since that time. In January 1952 the dominion bureau of statistics index of equipment was 218-1 (1935-39 = 100) and by January 1953 it had dropped to 207-7, a decline of five per cent.
I should like to set out the position in relation to beef cattle over the period. The beef cattle market recently has undergone an adjustment under the influence of heavy marketings and declining prices in the United States. Since the first of this year the inspected slaughter of cattle in the United States has been over 30 per cent above 1951, and prices there are about $12 per hundred below the price of February, 1952. The influence of this has been felt on the Canadian market since the removal of the United States embargo on March 2, 1953. The present price of good steers at Winnipeg is $9 below that of February, 1952, the last month before the United States embargo was imposed. Good steers at Chicago were selling at $32.20 a hundred in February, 1952, and $20.45 at the beginning of April, 1953. At Winnipeg, good steers sold at $27.92 in February, 1952 and $18.60 at the beginning of April, 1953.
The present position of the cattle market, however, must be considered in relation to the substantial price advances of recent years. The average price received by farmers at their primary shipping points for all grades was $9.63 a hundred pounds during the period 1943-45. During the period 1950-52 farmers received an average price of $23.78 a hundred pounds, which is two and a half times greater.

Although present cattle prices do represent an adjustment from those of the period 1950-52, they are somewhat higher than prevailed in 1949 and almost double those of 1943-45. The average price of good steers at Toronto was $21.07 in March, 1953 as compared with $19.89 in March 1949, $15.44 in March 1948, and the 1943-45 annual average of $11.64.
While net cattle marketings for the first three months of this year, at 348,825 head, are 45 per cent above a year ago, they are very close to those of 1951 when net marketings for the first three months were 335,537 head. It is of interest, however, that in the month of March this year exports of beef and beef cattle to the United States were equal to less than one thousand head of cattle compared to approximately 27,000 head in March 1951. The present marketings are, therefore, being very largely consumed in Canada with the result that while Canadian cattle prices have declined recently they still are somewhat above the level which would prevail if there was a substantial surplus being exported to the United States.
This trend toward an increased domestic use of beef was also apparent in 1952 when, in spite of the fact that total marketings were 100,000 head lighter than the year before, the net domestic use was 15 per cent heavier.
As a result of this increased domestic use and of the lighter marketings during 1952, the surplus purchased by the agricultural prices support board during the period of the United States embargo was kept within reasonable limits. Those purchases resulted in the shipment of approximately 70 million pounds of beef to the United Kingdom under the New Zealand diversion arrangement, and the board holds approximately 20 million pounds of beef in storage in Canada.
I should also like to state the position in relation to hogs over a similar period. The hog market at present is in a sound position. Reasonably heavy marketings are clearing well domestically and to export outlets in this hemisphere. Prices are equal to or better than those of a year ago, and a continuing firm market is expected through the spring and summer with active buying interest from the United States, where hog slaughter is down 13 per cent from last year.
Hog prices are maintaining reasonably well the advances made since the late war years. The average farm price for hogs for the years 1943 to 1945 was $16.63 per hundred pounds. This increased to an average of $27.27 for the years 1950 to 1952. The present price of $27.50 for grade A carcass hogs at Toronto

compares to an average April price of $22.47 in 1950, $32.45 in 1951 and $26 in 1952.
The basic strength of the hog market is being maintained in spite of the fact that marketings last year and this year are at or above the levels of most of the years through the 1940's when heavy reliance was placed on exports to the United Kingdom. The 1952 hog marketings, when over 61 million head were cleared through grading centres, was the third highest in Canadian history. It is estimated that 1953 gradings will be in the order of 5J million hogs, which will be 16 per cent above the average for 1946 to 1951.
The disposal of the 1952 marketings was, of course, handicapped by the existence of the United States embargo. However, all of the 64 million pounds of pork cuts and sides purchased by the agricultural prices support board in supporting hogs during 1952 have now been sold back into the market. Of the 98 million pounds of canned pork purchased by the board the remaining 71 million pounds are expected to be disposed of this year. The clearance of the heavy 1952 marketings was facilitated by the fact that domestic use of pork in 1952 from hogs slaughtered in grading centres was over 859 million pounds, which was 27 per cent higher than in 1951.
I should like also to make a statement with regard to eggs. The position of the egg market is being well maintained by the expanding Canadian economy and by export outlets in this hemisphere.
Commercial egg marketings in 1952 were 5 [DOT] 4 million cases, only 7 per cent less than the average for the years 1944 to 1949. During this period exports to the United Kingdom were at a high level, reaching as much as 2 [DOT] 9 million cases, or 87 million dozen, in one year. In those six years the average domestic use of eggs from commercial marketings was 3 [DOT] 5 million cases. In 1952 exports were 400 thousand cases and domestic use 5 million cases, or 43 per cent higher than the 1944-49 average.
Marketings in 1953 are expected to be 10 per cent under those of 1952. With present indications that chick hatches this spring will be no greater than those of a year ago, it is anticipated that production over the coming year will be well within the requirements of the Canadian market and of usual export outlets.
The average farm price of eggs for the years 1950-52 was 43 cents per dozen, compared to 31 cents for the years 1943-45. To date this year the average farm price has been 8 cents per dozen above 1952.
Milk production during 1952 amounted to 16-8 billion pounds, an increase of 361 million pounds or 2-2 per cent from 1951. This
Supply-Agriculture
increase is needed to maintain the present rate of consumption for the increased population in Canada. So far this year, milk production in Canada is approximately 5 per cent greater than a year ago. The December report of cow numbers in Canada shows there were 160,000 more dairy cows in Canada at that time than there were a year earlier. However, during the first six weeks since the United States embargo on cattle was lifted 7,436 dairy cattle were exported, which amount is 436 greater than during the corresponding period of 1951; that is during the year prior to the embargo imposed by the United States.
During 1952, the fluid milk and cream trade of cities and towns used 4,345 million pounds of milk as compared with 4,227 million pounds in 1951, an increase of 118 million pounds or nearly 2-8 per cent. This increase is equivalent to about 111 million pounds of cheese. Last year, 1952, almost 26 per cent of all milk produced in Canada was used for the city fluid milk trade as compared with 19 per cent before the war, in 1939. The above does not include milk consumed on the farm or fed to livestock which amounts to 15 to 16 per cent of the total production of milk and which varies very little from year to year. During January, 1953, there was an increase of 8 per cent in fluid milk and cream sales as compared with those of January, 1952.
The increase in the requirements of the fluid milk trade of the cities and towns of Canada is due mainly to increased population, and explains why less milk is available for the manufacture of other products. The fluid milk trade is the highest priced outlet for the producers of milk. During the years 1943-45 the average price to producers was $2.45 per 100 pounds, while in 1950-52 it averaged $3.92 or an increase of $1.47 per 100 pounds of milk.
Canadian creamery butter production has through the years been pretty much in line with domestic demands. It reached an alltime high in 1943, when it was 312 million pounds. Since 1949, following the introduction of margarine, production of butter declined each year to 257 million pounds in 1951, which is approximately the pre-war level. This lower trend was halted in 1952, when production of creamery butter amounted to 281 million pounds, or 24 million pounds greater than in 1951, equivalent to an increase of approximately 9 per cent. This increase in butter production has continued in 1953 and, so far this year, it is 24 per cent greater than during the corresponding period of 1952. In eastern Canada the

Supply-Agriculture
increase is due largely to diversion of milk from condenseries to butter and cheese factories.
Consumption of creamery butter in 1952 amounted to 274-7 million pounds as compared with 268-9 million pounds in 1951, an increase of 5-8 million pounds or approximately 2 per cent. Stocks of creamery butter as at April 1, 1953, were 26-6 million pounds as compared with 17 [DOT] 4 million pounds a year ago. This year the government holds 72 per cent of the butter stocks and the total holdings by both the government and the industry at April 1, 1953, were equivalent to only one month's supply.
Of the total milk production in Canada, almost 45 per cent is utilized in the manufacture of butter. During the years 1943-45 the average returns to producers for butter-fat used in making creamery butter was 43 cents per pound while in 1950-52 it was 61 cents, or an increase of 18 cents per pound of butterfat. The continuation of the support price for butter for another two years at the same level as that of the past two years will tend to stabilize the entire dairy industry.
Production of cheddar cheese in 1952 was 66 -6 million pounds as compared with 85-3 million pounds in 1951, a decrease of 18-7 million pounds or 22 per cent. Cheddar cheese is produced in every province of Canada except Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, but about 75 per cent is manufactured in Ontario and 18 per cent in Quebec. The cheese-producing areas of these two provinces are now also producing milk for condenseries, butter and powder factories and, to a considerable extent, the fluid milk plants in cities. Cheddar cheese production has declined from the wartime high of 207-4 million pounds in 1942 to 66-6 million pounds in 1952. The decrease in cheese production is due mainly to diversion of milk to other products, and this was especially noticeable in 1952.
Stocks of cheddar cheese as at April 1, 1953, were 26-2 million pounds as compared with 24-8 million pounds a year ago. Earlier this spring there were exports of slightly over 5 million pounds to the United Kingdom. The present stocks are about normal, as the industry usually holds approximately 25 million pounds in order to supply the public with cheese of varying degrees of ripeness such as mild, medium and old.
Consumption of cheese has been increasing gradually in Canada, and during 1952 the quantity of cheddar cheese used was 59-5 million pounds as compared with 57 [DOT] 8 million pounds in 1951 or an increase of 1-7 million pounds. The importance of expanded domestic markets is reflected in the price of cheese

milk to producers. During the years 1943-45, cheese producers received an average price of $1.91 per 100 pounds whereas in the years 1950-52 it was $2.37, an increase of 46 cents per 100 pounds.
Coming now to condensed milk products, production of these products has increased steadily during recent years and in 1952 it was the highest on record. Last year, 1952, the total production of both whole milk products-that is, evaporated milk, condensed milk, whole milk powder-and by-products, that is, dry skimmed milk, buttermilk powder, etc., amounted to 471 million pounds as compared with 435 million in 1951. This is an increase of 36 million pounds and is equivalent to 8-2 per cent. For the first time in the history of Canadian dairying this branch of the industry used a greater proportion of the total milk production than that used by the cheese factories; that is, concentrated milks 5-2 per cent, cheese 4-4 per cent.
The domestic market uses approximately 86 per cent of the concentrated milks produced in Canada and the remaining 14 per cent is exported to some 50 different countries throughout the world. Exports are being hampered by embargoes, quotas and currency difficulties. Domestic consumption of most products, however, continues to increase. In 1952 the Canadian market used 265 million pounds of evaporated milk as compared with 250 million pounds in 1951, an increase of 15 million pounds or 6 per cent.
Stocks of evaporated milk at April 1, 1953, were almost 23 million pounds as compared with 13 million a year earlier. These are being reduced and it is expected that by early May they will be normal for that time of year. The usual trading stocks are from 13 to 20 million pounds.
Dry skimmed milk and dry buttermilk were exported to the United States in former years. The embargoes placed on these and other products by the United States have reduced exports. However, other countries such as Mexico and Venezuela, to mention only two, are now taking substantial quantities of powdered milk with good prospects of further development. Domestic usage is also being increased, particularly in the baking trade and for household use. In the meantime the government has undertaken to purchase 10 million pounds of dry skimmed milk as a means of assisting the industry in adjusting itself to these changing conditions.
During the years 1943-44-45 the average price to producers of milk for evaporating purposes was $2.05 per 100 pounds, while in 1950-51-52 it was $2.83, an increase of 78 cents per 100 pounds.

I come now to ice cream, which is now utilizing almost 3 per cent of our total milk production which is 70 per cent of the amount used by the cheese industry. Last year there were 27 million gallons produced in Canada as compared to 9 million gallons before the war, that is in 1939.
Turning now to apples, the 1952 Canadian apple crop was comparatively light at 11-7 million bushels as compared with 13-6 in 1951 and the 5-year average, 1946 to 1950, of 16-5 million bushels. A generally good demand and a firm market prevailed throughout the season. Price levels in eastern Canada were much higher than those of the previous season and in western Canada were at about the same relatively high levels as in 1951-52. Export demand, largely from the United States, was quite good and total exports to March 31 of 2-1 million bushels were approximately equal to those of a year ago. Storage stocks on April 1 were 747,000 bushels as compared with the unusually light holdings of 683,000 bushels a year ago and the 5-year, 1947-51, average for April 1 of 1,130,000 bushels. Approximately half of the current holdings are in British Columbia and consist of Newtown and Winesap. Remaining stocks are expected to be cleaned up without difficulty.
Coming now to potatoes, production in 1952 was 58-9 million bushels, 22 per cent larger than the light 1951 crop of 48-3 million bushels. High prices from the short crop of 1951 were carried over into the fall of 1952. First estimates of 1952 production indicated another comparatively short crop, and although subsequent estimates were revised upward, growers generally appeared inclined to hold in anticipation of a repetition of the previous season's high levels. The market started to decline in the late fall and continued until mid-April, when the first indication of a firmer market was apparent. Despite the current low prices, however, the returns on potatoes sold during the season to March 31 in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick compare quite favourably with the record high levels of a year ago and are much above returns for earlier years. Price returns per bushel to growers in New Brunswick for bulk Canada No. 1 grade table stock show average returns August to March inclusive as follows:-
1949- 50	53 cents per bushel
1950- 51	32 cents per bushel
1951- 52	1.68 per bushel
1952- 53	1,39 per bushel
When the figures are looked at on a monthly basis they show that the price trends for this year and last are almost in reverse. In 195152 the August price for New Brunswick was
Supply-Agriculture
56 cents per bushel and for March $2.64 per bushel, with an average of $1.68 for the seven-month period. This year, 1952-53, the August price for New Brunswick potatoes was $2.52 per bushel and the March price 68 cents per bushel with an average of $1.39 per bushel. Should the present upward trend in potato prices continue it will of course influence the seasonal average returns.
The situation in the United States paralleled that in Canada. The market in the state of Maine declined and prices in some cases were below the levels prevailing in Canada. This contributed toward the decline in Canada and resulted in the importation into New Brunswick during the period February 1-April 16 of approximately 100,000 bushels of Maine potatoes. These, however, represent a very small proportion of Canadian exports to the United States of 2-5 million bushels this season to date. In considering trade with the United States it is well to remember that during the 10-year period 1943-52, inclusive, Canadian exports totalled 47-3 million bushels -seed 29 million and table stock 18 million- valued at $57 million, while imports from the United States totalled only 17 million bushels valued at $28 million.
These are the reviews that I wished to make of the situation in relation to many of the staple farm products that we have been discussing from time to time. There is one other matter that I wish to discuss with the committee. It is a matter we discussed to a considerable extent at the beginning of the session, and that is the larger irrigation projects.
I am afraid the opposition have made it most difficult for us to debate some questions properly under the rules. They forced a full-dress debate on the South Saskatchewan river project, and carried it to a vote. The question has, therefore, been debated during this session. To state the case is to indicate how useless it is to call such a division and how much damage it could do if the rules were strictly enforced.
However, there is an item in the estimates entitled "major irrigation and reclamation projects in the prairie provinces, $7,893,420." Included in this item is the South Saskatchewan river development. Under this item it would be possible to finance work on the project.
It is, therefore, important for me to stare the present position of the project. After considering thoroughly the information compiled and the views expressed in the report of the Hogg commission as well as the comments on it by the Saskatchewan government, this government has decided that we should

Supply-Agriculture
be prepared to review and continue our discussions with the government of Saskatchewan on the feasibility of the project as set up by P.F.R.A. and the willingness and ability of the provincial government to assume the costs of what we would consider provincial obligations.
In order to place before the committee the attitude we have assumed toward further discussions with the provincial government, I ask leave to read into Hansard a letter to the premier of Saskatchewan which has gone forward to him and which is as follows:
Ottawa, April 24, 1953. Hon. Thomas C. Douglas, M.A.,
Premier of Saskatchewan,
Regina, Sask.
Dear Premier Douglas:
My files indicate that following the receipt of a report from our engineers to the effect that it is possible to construct a dam on the South Saskatchewan river at Coteau creek I asked for and had an interview with your government on June 24, 1950.
It was my opinion that because the resources were under the control of the province this information should be made known officially to your government.
We appointed a committee of top officials and engineers associated with the Department of Agriculture to compile the information. Before this report was made public, I again reported to the provincial government on February 2, 1951, indicating that the committee agreed with our engineers that a dam could be built creating a reservoir and that the direct results from such a construction could be irrigation and power generation.
I indicated that the estimated cost of the project would be approximately $101,000,000 on a basis of 1950 costs, divided as follows: $65,000,000 for the dam, $25,000,000 for irrigation and $8,000,000 for power installation. My memory is that you contended that the federal government had left the impression that this was to be a federal undertaking financed by Ottawa. I pointed out that it had been nothing more than a proposal to assist in rehabilitating the drought area and that the only large projects which had been undertaken up to that time, namely, the St. Mary's and Bow river projects, were purely irrigation and the responsibility for financing them was three-way-the federal government stored or made available the water, the province distributed the water over the area and the farmers formed irrigation districts under provincial legislation to distribute the water to the land and administer the districts. I also pointed out that a very considerable part of the return from this development could be from power which would be utilized by the provincial power commission. You were still of the opinion that the federal government should pay the whole cost of the dam and I indicated that you might put your views in writing which you did on February 10.
The committee of officials reported on April 2, 1951. This report was made public and tabled in the house. There was some discussion in the house after which I answered your letter on June 26, 1951, to indicate that all the information was being referred to a committee of experts. This turned out to be a royal commission which reported on January 19, 1953.
The report has been tabled in the House of Commons and has given rise to very diverging views about the soundness of the project. Your government has prepared a document which is quite critical of the report and you have written

the Prime Minister that your government feels the project should be proceeded with notwithstanding the report of the royal commission.
Since this is your view, the federal government is prepared to consider a definite proposal from the provincial government for co-operation in the project and I am authorized by my colleagues to discuss such a proposal with you once the question of water rights has been settled among the three prairie provinces and agreement reached that the water would be available for the project.
Any proposal put forward by the province should make it clear what contribution to the cost of the dam itself the province is prepared to make to remove any element of federal subsidy for the production of power since power development could obviously not be subsidized in one province unless the federal authorities were prepared to provide similar subsidies in all provinces and federal subsidies for power development are contrary to present government policy.
You will appreciate that any federal contribution would also have to be limited, as in the St. Mary's and Bow river projects, to works for the conservation of the water and that we could not justify the expenditure of money raised from taxes all over Canada until the provincial authorities had prepared a practical scheme for the distribution system w'hich gave reasonable evidence that the water would actually be used for irrigation on a scale which would justify the expenditure of national funds.
Any proposal would, of course, have to include some satisfactory means of determining in advance what the total cost of the project would be, and what the federal share of the cost would be. This would be essential so that there was no open-ended commitment which might result in the final costs being far greater than anything either government would regard as reasonable.
On these conditions as prerequisites the federal government is prepared to discuss the project further with the government of Saskatchewan.
Yours sincerely,
James G. Gardiner.
This letter is signed by myself as Minister of Agriculture, on behalf of the government.
May I ask what date that was written?

The letter is dated April 24, 1953. It will be delivered today to the premier of Saskatchewan.
In concluding my remarks with regard to the estimates for this year I would point out that they are approximately the same as last year. There are of course variations in the different items, up or down slightly, but the amount which has been provided for expenditure during the coming year is approximately the same as it was last year. I submit these to the committee. They will be before you for discussion, and I shall be prepared to answer any questions anyone may ask with regard to my estimates.
For the present I would suggest that if anyone has any remarks to make or questions to ask I shall be prepared to try to answer the questions or listen to the remarks. I understand it is the intention to go on with

these estimates tomorrow after other items of business have been taken care of.
In connection with the figures that were placed on Hansard earlier, may I ask the minister in what year the Canadian embargo against cattle going into the United States was lifted?

The hon. member is not referring to the embargo because of foot-and-mouth disease which was placed on last
year?
The Canadian embargo.
That was lifted in August, 1948, I think.

The years used for comparison of cattle prices were 1943-45 and the present, and I think that was a most unfair comparison. The prices which existed in Canada during 1943-45 were as a result of this embargo imposed by the Canadian government. During those calendar years the difference between what the Canadian producer received for his livestock and coarse grains and the prevailing prices in the United States amounted to several hundreds of millions of dollars annually.

I purposely did not base any argument on anything I said. I simply produced the facts which are on the record, and I presume that when we come to the different items there will be considerable discussion. I doubt very much if this is the time to have a discussion on the facts. The facts are on the record and between now and the time we come to the particular item any hon. member can look them up and I presume that arguments such as the one just heard will be presented. We can then argue out this matter. I would hesitate to start an argument at five minutes to ten.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to speak at any length at this time because we had a considerable debate on agriculture two weeks ago. I want to commend the minister for sticking so closely tonight to his prepared script. I think he gave a more factual resume than we would ordinarily have got, and he has veered away from that ultra-optimistic attitude which he has taken on previous occasions.
I should like to go a little further than the hon. member for Souris and say that the comparison made by the minister does not apply only to beef, it applies to all farm products. The minister used as a comparison the period of 1943-45 and the present time, and that was most unfair. The period of 1943-45 was two years after the government froze all prices of farm products when they were extremely
Supply-Agriculture
low. Prices were frozen in 1941 and they were allowed to go up but very little between 1941 and 1943. Therefore to make a comparison between 1943-45 and 1949-52 is most unfair. I think everyone in and outside the house will realize that fact.
As I said previously, I commend the minister for sticking to the facts tonight in his statement. He gave us a very good picture of the agricultural situation. As he said, there has been a great increase in the production of most dairy products in this country. What we need to know is what the government is doing about getting rid of the surpluses that are developing.
I see the house leader, the Minister of Public Works, getting a little jittery, so I presume he wants to call it ten o'clock.
Item stands.
Progress reported.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, tomorrow we shall proceed with Bill No. 339, to amend the National Housing Act. The Minister of Resources and Development had intended to go to Lunenburg tomorrow to attend the funeral of the late Senator Duff. However, I had promised hon. members that I would call this item tomorrow, and the minister agreed to stay.
